extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, and patent litigators (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal analysis and practical guidance on interpreting dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. §112(d), and on how that statute interacts with the doctrine of claim differentiation in U.S. patent prosecution and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the invention / primary importance of claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The claims of a patent define the invention to which the patentee is entitled the right to exclude.’ Claims themselves—not the patent specification, dictionaries or extrinsic evidence—are 'of primary importance' in defining a patent's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claim language as the starting point and primary authority for scope. Use other claims as a source of enlightenment only after construing claim language; specification and extrinsic evidence may inform but should not override clear claim language. (Cites Phillips v. AWH Corp., 415 F.3d 1303.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation doctrine (negative and positive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a dependent claim that adds a particular limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation in question is not present in the independent claim ('negative' differentiation). Conversely, independent claims are deemed broader than their dependents so that if one infringes a dependent claim, infringement of its independent parent automatically follows ('positive' differentiation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differences among claims as a guide to meaning and scope. Claim differentiation can broaden independent claims based on dependent claim language, and is frequently relied upon by courts to construe claims more broadly (examples: Wright Med. Tech., Laitram, Robotic Vision). But be aware it is a presumption, not an absolute rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation is a guide, not a rigid rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim differentiation 'is a guide, not a rigid rule.' If a claim will bear only one interpretation, similarity among claims must be tolerated; the clear import of the specification or prosecution history can overcome the presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on claim differentiation where the specification or prosecution history clearly dictates a contrary construction. Courts resist jettisoning specification-based constructions in favor of claim-differentiation in ambiguous situations (cases: Laitram, Edwards Lifesciences, Netcraft, Marine Polymer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory text of 35 U.S.C. §112(d) for dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Current provision: '(d) Reference in Dependent Forms.—Subject to subsection (e), a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat §112(d) as a statutory requirement that defines when a claim is properly in dependent form and how it must be construed (i.e., incorpora­tion of parent claim limitations). Congress intended the provision to permit dependent claiming but also to set a procedural/substantive requirement for dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim must 'specify a further limitation' or be invalid (Pfizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim that does not 'specify a further limitation of the subject matter of the claim to which it refers' fails §112(d) and can be invalidated (Pfizer v. Ranbaxy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that each dependent claim both refers to an earlier claim and adds a further limiting element; failure to do so can render the dependent claim invalid. Courts will not rewrite claims to preserve validity. Example: Pfizer invalidated a dependent claim that merely recited subject matter outside the scope of its immediate parent and thus did not further limit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependency determined by substance, not form (Monsanto)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is dependent depends on the substance of the claim in light of §112(d), not merely on its customary dependent claim wording. A claim drafted in an unusual format can still be dependent if it refers to an earlier claim and adds a further limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the actual claim language and the statutory requirements to determine dependence; do not allow mere variations in wording or unconventional formatting to defeat a dependency that meets §112(d)'s substantive criteria (Monsanto Co. v. Syngenta Seeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: §112(d) can prevent using dependent claims to broaden independent claims (Zircon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112(d) can limit a patentee’s attempt to use the language of a dependent claim to broaden an independent claim when such a reading would make the dependent claim fail to further limit the parent (Zircon v. Stanley Black & Decker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about arguing that independent claims should be broadened based on dependent claims if that reading would violate §112(d). Consult specification and prosecution history to determine the proper meaning (Zircon: 'ratio' meant division per specification/prosecution history; dependent claims could not be used to expand to subtraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of analysis: apply §112(d) (validity of dependent claim) before claim differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying claim differentiation first would effectively guarantee the validity of dependent claims under §112(d) and render the statute a nullity. Therefore, §112(d) must be applied before invoking claim differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dependent/independent claim issues arise, courts and litigants should assess whether the dependent claim satisfies §112(d) before relying on claim differentiation to construe the independent claim. Do not let claim-differentiation presumptions sweep aside a statutory invalidity problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not construe claims to preserve validity except where ambiguity remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not construe claims to preserve their validity unless 'the court concludes, after applying all the available tools of claim construction, that the claim is still ambiguous' (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions motivated solely by an intent to save validity; only where a claim remains ambiguous after full claim-construction analysis should courts select a construction that preserves validity. This principle supports applying §112(d) first rather than using claim differentiation as a 'golden ticket' to validate dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO practice: §112(d) rejections are rare but possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In PTO prosecution practice, rejections under §112 paragraph (d) (now §112(d)) are uncommon; examiners rarely perform substantive invalid dependent-claim analyses, though isolated rejections occur (e.g., scrivener's errors, dependent claims that merely restate properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that lack of §112(d) scrutiny during prosecution insulates dependent claims from invalidity in litigation; courts may apply §112(d) even if the PTO overlooked the issue. Consider potential §112(d) vulnerabilities when drafting and prosecuting dependent claims.
